posts.title: Lego Blockly: Graphical Common Programming Environment Web App (Using Intuitive Blockly) for All Lego Robotic Platforms.
posts.text: Like this ? This is an RF to PF IR receiver - the tiny IR LED on the top left of the PCB is fun to play with! The entire thing is really low power. Well, today there are other components (such as the C3), but this thing goes right in front of a PF receiver or RCX/Scout. OK, the latter have RF TX and a PIC as well, as the PBricks do reply to incoming data. Everything fits nicely into 3 hollowed-out 2x4 bricks: When placing the IR LED more or less directly in front of any TSOP receiver, something like 1 kOhm as resistor for the LED is enough. The TSOP don't like to be flooded with IR light, as they easily saturate at such short distances. This is work from 2011 - 15 years ago . A C3 should really fit into 3 2x4s won't it? I believe there are even smaller ESPs, and you'd need only one GPIO emitting the 38kHz modulated PF frames ... like this "Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32C3 Tiny MCU Board"? You'd need an antenna, though. Fun times! Best Thorsten

posts.title: [Software] BricksChat: Generate buildable MOCs from your own parts and download instructions
posts.text: After the results are finished, my main test was whether giving a more detailed, exact description of what should be done is better than just a short prompt. The first prompt is modified from what I used to create my other models before. Detailed prompt: Generate a LDR model of a Lego spacecraft. Use around 100 parts. Give special care that parts don't clip into each other, i.e., that the model is fully buildable in real life in the same way you have generated the file. Try to make the model as detailed as possible. Take your time to validate that there is indeed no clipping and everything can be built like it is. After 12min 11sec, the model was finished as this: Studio's stability checker displays full stability and connectivity. My short prompt only included the spaceship part and 100 parts, so they are comparable. Only took 9min 39sec this time: To me, this looks better than the first one, but I'd say it's probably by chance and not due to the difference in prompt length. Again, Studio showed me nothing in terms of stability and connectivity. So after these tests, I'm even more impressed than I previously was. Definitely a good upgrade from what major AIs produced before, and I'm sure you can proudly call you the godfather of LEGO® AI. That being said, in the big picture it could destroy the Premium MOC market, for now it's a cool project though. And all that makes me even more interested how the backend part works, if you use some custom instructions and forward it to Claude or use some own AI, etc. And I'm also interested in how you plan to turn it even or even make a profit. Because I essentially just used more than 20 minutes of your server capacity or AI tokens for free. "Edit:" I just saw the plans, are you planning to solely use them? Digging more through the plans, am I correct I just used my two free builds and will never be able to create more? And on the note of the Studio plan, do note that you can't publish these on Rebrickable as MOCs (either Premium or free), there were lengthy discussions about it, all being answered by rule F1/P1: You must be the original designer of the model. Definitely a good thing to hear from the creator of such a tool! For your ideas: Depends on the size of the creator, but definitely worth it I think. Musn't even be an AI for everything and anything, I'd just use Google's Reverse Image Search. These could potentially help implementing it: https://support.google.com/websearch/thread/298580848/does-google-offer-a-reverse-image-search-api-through-a-programmable-search-offering-or-gcp?hl=en https://serpapi.com/google-reverse-image https://github.com/SOME-1HING/google-reverse-image-api For a test of my MOCs, I had no luck with it, but I'd think if someone would search for images of BrickArtisian's MOCs they wouldn't need to dig far down the results. And lastly, I think a discussion on the Rebrickable Forum could also grant you some inside. So I'd recommend to make a post over there as well.

posts.title: Lego Blockly: Graphical Common Programming Environment Web App (Using Intuitive Blockly) for All Lego Robotic Platforms.
posts.text: I decided to go with the irsend repeat count and tried with 2 repeat counts for a total of 3 frames per command. The additionnal delay is awful. Anyway, I implemented Compile Flags at the beginning of the sketches to let you configure what repeat Frame counts you want for your project. Defaults is 2 for PF IR (3 frames) and 0 for PF RF (1 frame) You can also disable PF IR TX, IR RX, or RF TX when you are not using them in your projects. You will find in https://github.com/BlissCA/lego-blockly/tree/dev/SketchArduino, a sketch for ESP-WROOM-32 and one for ESP32-C3. For ESP32: LegoPFIR_BLE_ESP_WROOM_32_V8 I DID clean up and removed previous versions. If you plan to use only RF, then you should set PF IR repeat count to 0 or disable PF IR TX. The delays of both PF IR and PF RF adds up so just disable or reduce at least the repeat frame count of unused features. EDIT: Actually, the response time for one command once in a while is not bad, the IR receiver will probably get the first frame and executes it. The other frames will just do nothing. But it you have 2 consecutives commands, for example, Turn motor ON fwd on Red port and Turn motor ON Rev on Blue port, the ESP32 bridge will first send 5 complete frames for first command and only after that, it will send the 5 frames of second command. So rather than seeing your 2 motors turning on at the same time, there will be about 0.5 to 1 sec delay between each action. Now I'm experimenting sending frames using interleave method. This will be more efficient for sure. Stay tuned :-) EDIT 2: Interleave method is implemented now and it is MUCH more efficient for consecutive commands with multipe frames per commands (which should not happen often). Interleave means, if we repeat 3 command frames for each command, if the ESP bridge receives 2 commands at the same time from blockly, the bridge willl send Cmd1 Frame1, Cmd2 Frame 1, Cmd1 Frame 2, Cmd2 Frame2, Cmd1 Frame3, Cmd2 Frame3... Rather than Cmd1 Frame1, Cmd1 Frame2, Cmd1 Frame 3, Cmd2 Frame1, Cmd2 Frame2, Cmd2 Frame 3.

posts.title: Help with identifying parts/sets!
posts.text: Hi John, what a great find! I’ve done some digging. Samsonite distributed LEGO in Canada until 1988, which explains the bilingual box. The odd thing is that “65” doesn’t match any 1978 set I can find. In the Samsonite listings, 065 is an unrelated 1960s Garage Door set, so yours may simply never have been catalogued. Canadian sets often had their own numbers, different from the European versions with similar box pictures. A couple of suggestions: The member LEGO Historian has researched Canadian Samsonite sets in depth and has scans of the Canadian catalogues from 1976 onwards. It might be worth tagging or messaging him. To get it registered, Brickset and BrickLink both accept new set submissions. Clear photos of all box sides, plus the piece list or instructions if you have them, will help a lot. Would love to know what you find out!

posts.title: So, what Do people want?
posts.text: Great question, and I agree on parts pricing. Mine comes from a slightly different angle, as I mostly buy and sell secondhand LEGO. What I want is better support for the huge amount of LEGO already out there. Millions of sets are sitting in lofts and tubs, nearly complete. Make it easy to finish them: Every part in a set’s inventory actually available to buy, at a sensible price, for years after the set retires. Older instructions and inventories kept online forever. They’re brilliant now, and I hope that never changes. Part numbers printed or moulded somewhere visible, or an official way to identify a loose part, as anyone who’s sorted a job lot knows the pain. It would be better for the planet too: every completed secondhand set is one less new one needed. I’m with you on the competitors. The quality gap has closed a lot, and price is going to matter more and more.

posts.text: That is true. But EB is not a personal website. Remember, when you and I inquired for the TC Controller (IBM XT) software at the Billund Archives, after every other inquiry went nowhere? TLG officials responded, "Sorry, we can't provide you with access to that software, as it is IP protected". After >months<. I was so pissed about that reply, but it is what it is. We just don't want to gain their attention, do we? If we change source code because "we" can - and they still tell us it is theirs—I'd be careful. Why? I just cleared (couple of hours ago) a payment of €6150 from our non-profit (research) organization I happen to be the president of to an individual, because in 2019, we happily hosted a flyer on our website, advertising a scientific meeting in Cologne. That PDF showed a building of the University of Cologne. But an architect "owned" the photograph. It was on the internet, of course. He is an a*hole, definitely, but after a serious legal exchange (his lawyers, our lawyers), we paid the money. Originally, he asked for 10k. So we saved about 4k. But lost 6k for travel grants for young scientists. May sound pathetic, but believe me, I have become alert in such matters. And very careful. At least in the EU. Best Thorsten

posts.title: Lego Blockly: Graphical Common Programming Environment Web App (Using Intuitive Blockly) for All Lego Robotic Platforms.
posts.text: Oh yes! I was thinking along these lines, once I learned about the minimal footprint ESPs, you showed me. There is a caveat, though - I believe: When I was wandering into the RF world (well before 2010), I had an active "sensor" type RF extension for my RCX' in mind. Actually, that was the whole plan. RCX "active inputs" can provide sustained 10 mA of current at 5V. This is also what active RCX/Mindstorms/Int.B sensors are limited to. The LINX RF receiver operates well below that current at 3.3V. A simple resistor takes care of the 5V to 3.3V reduction, as per LINX documents. That was the reason for me to choose the LINX RF components. My active RF sensors I wanted to make for the RCX had further current sinking components: A microcontroller (microchip's >very small< PIC series) and an RF transmitter, as this "sensor" I had in mind was supposed to send back RCX message "acknowledgements". So the sensor was essentially a transceiver. Consuming less than 10 mA of current. That was back in the early 2000s. Now, about 2 decades later, well, new components became available. The C3 or other ESP varieties can be powered through the VIN pin as this goes either directly to the 3.3V low drop regulator or via a diode to that pin. The PF receiver delivers about 4V DC at the VCC pin of the TSOP. That may well work through ESP VIN. I have no clue though, how much current the PF receiver delivers at that pin. ESPs are quite current-hungry, as they have so many gadgets on board. This needs to be checked out! Another caveat: When you just solder a GPIO to the TSOP data pin, it may cause damage, when (accidentally) IR light is received. The TSOP output is open collector, the ESP GPIOs are not. So they may fight each other. In this case, I'd desolder the TSOP from the PF receiver. Everything should work absolutely fine, though. It would be a blast to have a C3 on a PF receiver. I am ready for any adventures; I even have an "open" PF receiver ready for surgery. Best Thorsten

posts.text: In the following statement in the void loop(): irsend.sendLegoPf(outFrame, 16, 0); you may change the 0 (repeat count) to 2 (Default for the remote handset from what I read). I think I refrained using the repeat count > 0 because it takes about 70-150 ms for 5 repeats (repeat count =4). And since IRremoteESP8266 irsend is a Blocking function, if my blockly programs sends 2 consecutive commands, the second command will have to wait for the first command to finish sending its 5 frames... However, I could use the irsend with repeat count = 0, in 5 loop scan, checking each time if a new command supersedes the processing command. I always try to make NON blocking code in a Bridge to make it as responsive as possible. I will try to do something with 3 repeats, in an unblockling way. For the IR distance thing, I believe now with a PF IR BLE Bridge, we can always put the bridge near the PF receivers since we now have the "BLE" for the long distance aspect with the Host. That is also why, I think, the RF thing is not necessary according to me. BLE does this job. With a very small ESP32-C3 or S3, you could bring the bridge right close the the IR receiver and could even use your hacked IR receiver and use the +, -, Data and wire it to the ESP32-C3 (Does it support 3.3v?). It would then directly use the new Unmodulated data pin I now provide. I will have to add the unmodulated pin to my official ESP32-C3 sketch.

posts.text: The code I used on my MulPI ESP32 for PF is stolen (OK, I asked before I used it, so it is copied with permission) from the LEGOINO software, Cornelius Munz made some time ago. It is still on GitHub, no idea whether you saw that. LEGOINO also sends out 5 repeated frames/single PF command. I believe they do that, because IR is not that reliable in "changing light" environments = ambient light rooms etc. :D In the PowerFunctions.cpp of LEGOINO, this section is calculating the pause between the 5 frame transmissions, I believe: // Pause function see "Transmitting Messages" in Power Functions PDF void PowerFunctions::pause(uint8_t count, uint8_t channel) { uint8_t pause = 0; if (count == 0) { pause = 4 - (channel + 1); } else if (count < 3) { // 1, 2 pause = 5; } else { // 3, 4, 5 pause = 5 + (channel + 1) * 2; } delayMicroseconds(pause * 77); //MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH } Well, it may not be necessary at all, when you have good lighting conditions! Best Thorsten

posts.text: Since devices motor blocks ask to turn on or turn off "Outputs", if the program finishes with outputs still ON, the stop button can then be used to extinguish all Outputs... The One Output PF Block send one command to one output and the PF IR Receiver retains this command. The Combo (2) outputs PF block on the other hand sends a command to both outputs but the receiver turns off the motors after few seconds if you don't keep sending the command... The Stop button sends 4 frames to cover all 4 possible channels.

posts.title: Lego Blockly: Graphical Common Programming Environment Web App (Using Intuitive Blockly) for All Lego Robotic Platforms.
posts.text: @Bliss Got out my oscilloscope. It does exactly what I envisioned: The 38 kHz modulated PF signal frame is present on GPIO 4, the non-modulated frame on GPIO 17. The envelope of a 38kHz signal on GPIO 4 (e.g. bit = 1) is exactly the same (duration) as the pure bit = 1 signal on GPIO 17. The modulated signal is emitted first on GPIO 4. With a delay of 78 ms the non-modulated signal follows on GPIO 17. When using the PFIR single port block, at default power level 4, the PF frame is emitted once on both outputs upon pressing "run". Motor spins. When adding a 2 s wait block and another PFIR single port block, brake, the PF frame is emitted once on both outputs. Motor stops. When only one single port block was executed (motor spins), pressing "stop", 4 identical PF frames are sent out on both outputs. A PF motor connected to a PF receiver/battery is doing exactly the right thing (on/off) every time I press run/stop. It thus runs perfectly well!!! I have to solder the data line of a LINX 433 MHz TX module to port 17 - this I shall do tomorrow! Remaining question: In normal LEGO Blockly program operation, every PF frame is sent out only once. Only when the program itself is stopped (i.e., not using a block), 4 PF stop frames are sent out. This is as you want/programmed it, Yves, correct? Man, you are my hero! All the best Thorsten EDIT: I just saw the "luxury settings"(!) at the beginning of the sketch - I did not read your post carefully enough! This is so cool. My LINX trasmitter wants 1 = H for sending a mark = 433Mhz carrier on - so default should work!

posts.title: [Software] BricksChat: Generate buildable MOCs from your own parts and download instructions
posts.text: Hi everyone, I built BricksChat and released it this week, it is an app which is like GPT, but for designing MOCs. I tried hard to avoid the "AI slop" problem and developed it in a way to generate actually valid buildable designs in 3D (including source .ldr/.mpd files and pdf instructions) from real parts. Moreover it also checks them against existing and official sets or MOCs in the catalogue for originality (including parts and subassemblies) to disclose a percentage of how much of it was copied (and the AI can be steered to attempt full originality and prevent copying from any existing sets). Or you can prompt it to copy explicitly to so a modification of your existing build, alt-build or combination of multiple sets. You can write a prompt like "design a set looking like this castle", attach an image and even specify a parts list (or sets you already own) to let it design what you can actually build from what you have at home right now. It is still an early prototype, but I was surprised how well it worked compared to what I've seen AI producing before. I wanted to share it here with you to give it a try. Web: https://brickschat.com/ What is currently on my backlog: Improving instruction generation (both pdf and interactive instructions) – I am not yet happy with the current quality and want to improve it ASAP. In case of big builds its not reliable at all. Proficiency in build techniques – Btw its already quite good incl. SNOTs, Technic mechanisms etc. But still not close in quality to human designed sets Improving speed & performance. Possibility to order the parts needed. Mobile app Let me know what other features would you like to prioritize! And share a link or photo of what you have built with it. For full transparency, this is my project and it has both free access and paid options: so far its very resource intensive, so I will see if it can pay to at least cover its own server bill. Thanks! Mirek PS: It is potentially very good at routing users to human designed MOCs (it always checks if anything with the similar topic already exists). If you are a creator, here is a waitlist https://brickschat.com/creators PS2: Is anyone interested in how it actually works from the AI side & github and so? It is not yet released & I am gauging the interest https://github.com/brickschat-com/brickschat-harness
